Considering the current geopolitical landscape, the conspicuous absence of Russia from the Global Peace Summit, and the lack of recognition of any proffered "peace initiatives" speaks volumes. The narrative of this conflict, as it's being shaped and disseminated, is one where Russia is painted as the aggressor, the instigator of turmoil, and therefore, unfit to be a credible peacemaker. This framing, meticulously crafted and amplified by Western media and international organizations, has effectively marginalized Russia. The Summit, designed to address the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, seems to have deliberately excluded any input or participation from the very nation at the heart of it. One could posit that the very premise of the event necessitates a dialogue that Russia is simply not allowed to be a part of, effectively nullifying any potential for a truly global, inclusive discourse on the matter. It’s a strategic move, no doubt, and yet, one can’t help but wonder about the long-term implications of such an exclusionary approach. It feels like a missed opportunity, a perpetuation of a cycle where communication is replaced by grandstanding, and cooperation is sacrificed at the altar of political expediency.

Text: Do Russians prefer Marine Le Pen over Emmanuel Macron in the upcoming French presidential election? Just 8 days ago, Russia’s RIA Novosti was gleefully celebrating, “Marine Le Pen buried Emmanuel Macron.” Last night, the Russian news were at a loss, not knowing how to comment on the fact that Marine Le Pen’s party lost not only to Macron’s centric alliance, but got beaten by the leftist “Popular Front”. The Kremlin didn’t prepare instructions for propagandists for such a case. But it was fixed overnight, and the Kremlin spin sounds as “France is finished”. In Kremlin’s version, it’s not Marine Le Pen that is “finished”, but the whole big country of France. Kremlin propagandists accused Macron in disregarding “the expression of the people’s will” — yes, this comes from the country where any opinion against the government gets you either in jail or grave — depending on Putin’s mood in the morning. An interesting background on Marine Le Pen is that her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, was a co-founder of the far-right party she was representing in the last 2 French presidential elections. The “National Front” party, which initially included Nazi-era collaborators, had been convicted multiple times for antisemitic hate speech and described the Holocaust as “a detail” of WWII history. However, in 2002, Le Pen Senior advanced into the 2nd round of presidential stand off against Jacques Chirac. That was the moment in French electoral history where the terrified French voters said, “Non!”, overwhelmingly rejecting Le Pen, with even the fans of the left voting to put Chirac, a conservative, in the Elysee Palace. Since then, French political parties used the tactic consistently against the far-right. The same strategy helped to consolidate centrist and leftist voters in the July 7 snap parliamentary elections, when Le Pen’s party only scored the 3rd, behind the leftist coalition and Macron’s alliance. Marine Le Pen’s father, who is now 96, left the big politics 13 years ago, in 2011. His party never won presidential elections. Following in his footsteps, Marine Le Pen participated in 2012, 2017 and 2022 presidential elections, losing them all. After her loss in 2022 presidential elections, Marine Le Pen handed the leadership to 26-year-old Jordan Bardella. He became the first person without the Le Pen name to lead the “National Front” since its founding in 1972. On the campaign trail, Le Pen and Bardella have presented themselves as “running mates”, with Le Pen vying for the presidency while pushing her protege for the position of prime minister. Obviously, Russian propagandists didn’t see Bardella as a proper leader, continuing to refer to Marine Le Pen as the leading force in the party. Yes, the leaders of the Russian regime are bitterly disappointed that Le Pen’s party didn’t win — they have already purchased expensive French champagne to celebrate (and its not a figure of speech — Google “Russians drink champagne for Donald Trump’s victory”). But they are hopeful that the leader of the leftist party that scored the majority of seats in the parliament will also interfere with France’s participation in NATO and especially with helping Ukraine. The hope expressed by pro-Putin commentators under the posts about Le Pen’s party loss is that “Melenchon will be even worse for Ukraine”, which means automatically, it will be better for Russia. 72-year-old Jean-Luc Mélenchon is a founder of left-wing ‘France Unbowed’ party. He became the self-appointed figurehead of the alliance comprised of — in addition to his own party — the Socialist Party, the French Communist Party as well as green, center-left and left-wing political groups, which scored the most number of seats in the parliamentary elections. The Russian propagandists keep their hopes up. Then, there’s the ever-present spectre of the “West” — that amorphous, nebulous entity that serves as the ultimate boogeyman in the Kremlin's narrative. Any setback for the West, any crack in its perceived unity, is cause for unbridled elation in Moscow. And France, with its rich history, powerful economy, and pivotal role in European affairs, is a prime target for this kind of gleeful opportunism. The Russian media, controlled entirely by the state, never misses an opportunity to exploit divisions, amplify dissent, and generally sow discord. They have honed this skill to a fine art, and the ongoing French political imbroglio is a veritable field day for them. It's all part of a bigger game, a relentless campaign to undermine the West from within. And, as history has repeatedly shown, it's a game the Kremlin is all too willing to play.

Text: How do Russian pilots drop glide bombs? It’s not that easy to find out, as the Russian Ministry of Defense keeps this information classified. Videos of Russian jets dropping glide bombs on Ukrainian territories have been circulating on the internet for almost two years. The tactic is simple: a guided bomb is dropped from a considerable distance from the target, gliding towards it. When the bomb is released, the aircraft, being at a safe distance from the target, is not subject to air defense attacks. Russia uses the FAB-series bombs for its glide bombing campaigns, notably FAB-500, FAB-1500, and FAB-3000. With a “kit” attached, a regular “dumb” bomb turns into a precision-guided munition. The bomb is fitted with wings that extend after the release, guided by a GPS system. The bombs are relatively cheap to manufacture and deploy, especially when compared to cruise missiles, making them an extremely effective weapon for Russia. Russian pilots use Su-34 fighter-bombers and Su-35 multirole fighters to drop these glide bombs. A video of a Ukrainian attack on a Russian air base in Crimea which showed the explosions of a Russian Su-30SM fighter jet and a Mig-29 fighter jet confirms that these planes can be targeted even at a safe distance. This gives Ukraine’s air defense a good reason to get Western weapons and strengthen their air defense capabilities. The war in Ukraine created an additional motivation for Russia to modernize the system. While it's cheaper than cruise missiles, the use of glide bombs is not without limitations, because the pilot has to fly in range of Ukrainian anti-aircraft defenses, and the bombs are susceptible to jamming. However, the large amount of glide bombs dropped demonstrates that the pros outweigh the cons for the Russian military.

Text: If Vladimir Putin learned he only had a few weeks to live, would he nuke the USA? The question itself is a morbid thought experiment, the kind that fuels late-night conversations fueled by cheap vodka, or, perhaps, high-brow philosophical debates in dimly lit university halls. Could a man, stripped of the illusion of immortality that most leaders cling to, resort to such a catastrophic act? Considering Putin's track record, the answer is not straightforward. The rumors surrounding his health, the way he isolates himself, the level of control he exerts – all paint a picture of a man terrified of the unknown. But fear, as any student of history will tell you, can manifest in unpredictable ways.  On one hand, the meticulously crafted image of the strongman, impervious to weakness, might crumble under the weight of mortality. The carefully constructed narrative of Russia's resurgence could be shattered, leaving him with nothing but ashes and a legacy of ruin. In such a scenario, a final, desperate act of destruction, a "go down with the ship" mentality, wouldn’t be entirely out of character. It would be, in a twisted way, a final assertion of power, a declaration that if he couldn't have the world, no one could.  However, there's another, equally plausible, interpretation. Putin isn't just a dictator; he's a pragmatist. He understands the delicate balance of power, the terrifying implications of nuclear war. He’s cultivated an image not just of strength, but also of strategic brilliance. He understands consequences more than most, given his history of KGB training. Launching a nuclear strike would not only obliterate the United States but would also condemn Russia to annihilation. It’s a move that wouldn't be about power itself, but sheer madness.

Text: Why does the current Russian military seem so incompetent? The ineptitude of the Russian military, as demonstrated in the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, is a source of bewilderment. It's a stark contrast to the image meticulously crafted by Russian propaganda over the years, depicting a formidable, almost invincible fighting force. The reality, however, is far more… complicated, and, frankly, embarrassing for the Kremlin. The issues seem to stem from several interconnected factors, a veritable Gordian knot of failures that have hamstrung their operations.  Corruption, for one, is a malignant tumor that has metastasized throughout the entire system. The pilfering of funds, the embezzlement of resources, the shady deals – all these practices have eroded the military's ability to function effectively. Equipment is substandard, supplies are inadequate, and the morale of the troops is in the gutter. Moreover, the quality of leadership appears sorely lacking. Commanders are seemingly chosen for their loyalty to Putin, not their strategic acumen or battlefield experience. This results in poor decision-making, reckless tactics, and a staggering disregard for the lives of Russian soldiers. The focus seems to be less on winning and more on maintaining control, a symptom of the broader authoritarian grip on power. This breeds a culture of fear and silence, where criticism is swiftly punished and incompetence is rewarded, perpetuating a cycle of failure. The initial planning for the invasion was shockingly naive, a gamble that has backfired spectacularly. The subsequent adjustments, characterized by brutal assaults, heavy losses, and a dependence on outdated strategies, suggest a military struggling to adapt to the realities of modern warfare. Indeed, the whole debacle is a monumental embarrassment, a tragedy of epic proportions, and a stark reminder of the devastating consequences of unchecked power and endemic corruption. It is a story of hubris, miscalculations, and the tragically unavoidable consequences of incompetence on a grand scale.

The video likely caused significant consternation within Russia, and its effects were widely discussed. It's quite probable that many Russians felt a complex mixture of emotions, including shame, anger, and a profound sense of humiliation. The images of their soldiers, often portrayed as paragons of strength and masculinity, yielding to Ukrainian forces directly contradicted the state-sponsored narrative of invincibility. The very essence of Putin's propaganda, carefully constructed to bolster national pride and project an image of military superiority, was undermined in an instant. The perception of weakness, particularly in the context of a war that was supposed to be a swift operation, would have been a bitter pill to swallow for many, especially those who believed the hype. The carefully cultivated image of the "strong Russian man," so central to the Kremlin's messaging, took a brutal hit. This narrative was carefully constructed to contrast the allegedly weak, decadent West with a strong, traditional Russia. Therefore, the sight of their own soldiers surrendering would have hit particularly hard. The impact, I suspect, reverberated through the social media, especially the pro-war channels, with the desperate search for explanations and the frantic attempts to spin the embarrassing reality. The Kremlin's reaction, likely, would have been swift.

Text: Which country has better military technology, Ukraine or Russia/USSR? Since the beginning of the full-scale war in Ukraine, we've been bombarded with claims about military might, technological supremacy, and the effectiveness of various weapons systems. The reality, as always, is far more nuanced.  Initially, the narrative painted a picture of a technologically superior Russian army, laden with advanced weaponry. However, the battlefield has revealed a different story. While Russia undoubtedly possesses some impressive military hardware, its effectiveness has been repeatedly hampered by logistical failures, poor training, and questionable tactical decisions. The Russian military, at least during the first year of the war, appeared to be fighting on a shoestring, with basic equipment and outdated supply chains.  Conversely, Ukraine, despite being significantly outmatched in terms of sheer numbers and overall resources, has demonstrated a remarkable ability to utilize Western-supplied weaponry effectively. The Ukrainians have shown extraordinary ingenuity and adaptability in employing these systems, turning the tide of battle on multiple occasions. They’ve mastered the art of asymmetric warfare. The use of drones, for instance, has been a game-changer, with both sides adopting them on a massive scale.  It's not just about the technology itself but also about how it's utilized. The Russians, often hampered by bureaucracy and rigid hierarchies, have struggled to adapt to the ever-changing battlefield reality. The Ukrainians, by contrast, have demonstrated a level of flexibility and innovation that has allowed them to maximize the effectiveness of the weapons they have.  It’s a brutal, bloody conflict, no matter how advanced or primitive the weaponry. The war has shown that military technology alone doesn't guarantee victory; it is a whole picture, starting from a strong army, continuing with good training, excellent coordination, and brave soldiers. And let’s not forget the motivation to fight.  In terms of the USSR, the question becomes even more complex, as the Soviet Union, at its peak, boasted a military-industrial complex that was arguably on par with, if not surpassing, its Western counterparts. However, the collapse of the Soviet Union led to a decline in military capabilities for all former Soviet republics, included Russia. Many of the technologies of the USSR are in the museums now.

Text: What would make people laugh at Putin? It seems the court jester routine doesn’t quite fit. The Russian leader, a man who cultivates an image of steely resolve and calculated power, is hardly known for his comedic timing. Yet, the internet, that unruly beast, finds humor where it can. The memes are relentless, of course. Images of Putin riding bears, bare-chested, or glaring menacingly circulate endlessly. These, however, are not laugh-out-loud funny. They are cynical, born of a grim reality. True humor, the kind that cuts deep, requires a certain level of vulnerability, something Putin studiously avoids. To really make people laugh *at* Putin, you’d need to expose a chink in his armor. A genuine blunder, a moment of self-doubt, a recognition of failure — these would be the comedic gold. Imagine a scenario where his carefully constructed facade crumbles, even for a fleeting second. Picture him tripping on the red carpet, forgetting his carefully rehearsed lines, losing his teleprompter mid-speech. Such gaffes would be amplified across the globe, echoing through news outlets and social media, becoming instant memes and fueling mocking laughter. The world, exhausted by his brand of authoritarianism, would relish such a spectacle. However, this genuine, spontaneous humor is exactly what Putin’s carefully constructed reality seeks to extinguish. He meticulously controls the narrative, curating every image, every word, every public appearance. It’s a high-stakes game of image management, and right now, Putin’s determined to maintain a poker face, even if it means sacrificing genuine laughter. He understands, perhaps better than anyone, that a single misstep could unravel his carefully constructed edifice of power. And that, ironically, is what makes people want to laugh at him even more. His fear of ridicule is his greatest vulnerability and would be the fuel for a thousand satirical memes.

The architects of this misinformation campaign fail to grasp that the truth, however painful, always prevails.

Text: Here in the west we hear all kinds of things about Russia. What is it really like to live there? Is Putin liked and/or respected? Do Russians have a better life than they used to? It's difficult to ascertain a unified sentiment, given the vastness of the country and the multifaceted nature of its populace. However, a prevailing narrative, disseminated by those in power, paints a picture of stability and national pride. One could argue that Putin enjoys a certain level of respect, cultivated over years of carefully crafted propaganda. He’s presented as a strong leader navigating treacherous international waters, the stalwart defender of Russia's interests. The state-controlled media relentlessly promotes this image, consistently portraying him as a savior in a world allegedly hostile to Russia.  As for quality of life, it’s a complex issue. The narrative promoted by the Kremlin showcases grand infrastructure projects, increased wages (at least, in some sectors), and a general sense of prosperity. Yet, such a rosy picture often obscures glaring disparities. A sizable portion of the population struggles daily, grappling with economic hardship and limited opportunities. Furthermore, the erosion of civil liberties and the crackdown on dissent create a climate of fear and uncertainty. Historically, life in Russia has always been a balancing act of resilience and adaptation, and today is no exception. Whether Russians enjoy a better life than before is thus a matter of perspective, greatly influenced by one's socio-economic standing and access to information. Text: What is the name of the new Kursk Republic? Is it Kursk People's Republic or just Kursk Republic? When is the referendum for the separation from the Russian Pederation? Have you seen the flag of this new country? These questions, proliferating online, are reminiscent of the feverish speculation that swirled around the so-called “Donetsk People’s Republic” and “Luhansk People’s Republic” a decade prior. No, there is no new “Kursk Republic.” No, there will be no referendum. No, you haven’t seen its flag because it doesn't exist, and likely never will. The origin of such queries is quite predictable – a mischievous blend of misinformation, wishful thinking, and, perhaps, genuine geopolitical ignorance, all stirred up by various actors with vested interests. The world is a chaotic place, and the information ecosystem is even more so, yet the desire to find easy, quick answers for complex issues is very strong. The human brain tends to gravitate towards simplicity, crafting convenient narratives that fit within a predetermined framework. In regards to the “Kursk Republic”, this framework is the narrative of a fractured Russia, a weakened adversary easily carved up into smaller, more manageable pieces. This framing is a fantasy, a convenient delusion of those who seek the disintegration of the Russian Federation. And yet, even in the absence of reality, these fantasies have consequences; they create an illusion of inevitability, stirring up false hopes and igniting misguided animosity. In the realm of international relations, truth is always complicated; the notion of a neatly divided Russia, or any other nation, is a simplistic fantasy, and not something to be taken seriously.

Text: What should Russians stop doing immediately? Russians should immediately stop believing the propaganda. And that is easier said than done. For decades, the Russian people have been fed a steady diet of lies, distortions, and outright fabrications, all designed to keep them docile and compliant. The state-controlled media, the textbooks, the history lessons – they all paint a picture of a glorious past and a victimized present, with the West as the eternal enemy. Breaking free from this mental cage is a Herculean task, requiring a constant questioning of everything, a willingness to seek out alternative sources of information, and an unwavering commitment to the truth. The irony is that, at least in the past, finding the truth about anything was almost impossible. Soviet citizens had to rely on the "Radio Free Europe" for news. If you were particularly curious, you could face severe repercussions — at best, a loss of your job. At worst, the label of "traitor to the Motherland" and a lengthy stay in a Siberian camp. People are still afraid, and with very good reason.

Text: How good is Putin in using nationalism or patriotism for his gain? Since 2022, Putin and his propagandists promote the idea of dying to get more land for Russia as the most important thing for any citizen. At first, Putin was blunt, stating to mothers of soldiers that it’s better for their sons to die in Ukraine from shrapnel wounds or bullets than from drinking bootleg alcohol or in a car crash. Then in 2023, propagandist Vladimir Solovyov (who might soon get an arrest warrant from Hague international court for crimes against humanity — for his bloodthirsty propaganda rants) was insisting one shouldn’t be afraid of death. “Life is greatly overrated,” Solovyov proclaimed on state TV to the audience of millions. “Life is greatly overrated. Why be afraid of what is inevitable?” Solovyov was trying to be convincing. Now Putin calls for Russians to volunteer to go to war, without sparing their lives and health, stating that’s what patriotism is. (Video in the comments below.) Apparently, the only problem Putin has — he can’t find the right words, which would convince Russian men to do it. He's trying hard. Yet, the results of his "patriotic" efforts are rather lackluster. He is facing a severe shortage of manpower, with those willing to fight dwindling and the ones being conscripted actively fleeing the country. Meanwhile, a Russian soldier says that things in Putin’s army aren’t great at all. The recruiters are happy to send to the front anyone — aged, crippled, unprepared, and drug addicts. The attitude of the commanders is terrible: “They just throw in as meat those without an eye, without fingers…” This is patriotism “Russian style”, young man. The more suffering, the more death, the more patriotic citizen of mother Russia you are. Putin’s “patriotic” agenda reveals itself: instead of a glorious victory, Russia is experiencing the collapse of its army, with many soldiers forced into the conflict against their will or without proper training. If the war against Ukraine continues for a long time, Vladimir Putin will learn the hard way that a nation cannot be built on nationalism and cynicism, and for sure, Vladimir Putin did not understand this.

Text: Is it true that Vladimir Putin brought a Labrador to a meeting with Angela Merkel because she's afraid of dogs? This juicy tidbit, like so many from the Kremlin, is multifaceted. The story itself is probably apocryphal, a delightful blend of rumor and speculation. But the very fact that it circulates, that it has legs in the media, is far more telling than the veracity of the anecdote itself. The subtext of the narrative is clear: Putin, the master strategist, understands the weaknesses of his opponents and, with a carefully orchestrated gesture, exploits them. Merkel, the iron lady, rendered vulnerable by a simple four-legged creature? It plays into the grand narrative of Putin as a cunning, almost Machiavellian, political actor. The reality, as with most things emanating from the Russian leadership, is undoubtedly more intricate and less theatrical. Still, the image has value. The story, like any good propaganda, works on multiple levels, appealing to various audiences. Some find it amusing, a bit of harmless political gossip. Others see it as evidence of Putin's ruthlessly tactical approach to international relations. Regardless of the truth, the widespread dissemination of such stories underscores a key element of the Kremlin's playbook: the manipulation of perception.
